summary:
Ben Hylak, founder of Dawn, presents on designing unbounded products in the age of multimodal AI. He defines unbounded products as those transcending the traditional mouse-and-monitor paradigm, citing his experience in robotics, SpaceX rockets, and four years designing visionOS for Apple Vision Pro. AI amplifies this unboundedness by accepting text, voice, images, video, and even emotional inputs like pleading or confiding, but this creates unpredictability—users assume false capabilities, try them, fail, and leave. Most non-technical users learn via word of mouth rather than trial and error, making good design critical.

Hylak organizes his talk around past, present, and future. For the past, he shares three lessons from Vision Pro: (1) highlight what matters and do it fast, (2) establish hierarchy to give unbounded products shape and purpose, and (3) leverage familiarity. For the present, he examines AI product design patterns. Good patterns include Dot's journal-like structure, Perplexity's search-engine-like layout, Claude's artifacts pulling structured output into a side panel, and version control patterns (ChatGPT's edit-message tree, Vercel v0's iteration UI). A bad anti-pattern is embedding ephemeral UI sliders inside chat. He adds that Clay demonstrates the only real-world agent use case—spreadsheets where each column is an agent step, run like evals across rows. Examples and presets (ChatGPT suggestions, V0's explore page, Notion's tone menu) help users skip prompt engineering.

For the future, Hylak argues prompt engineering will diminish—Linus described it as driving a car with a pool noodle from the back seat. Apple's generative image UI and Figma's tone adjustment show intuitive alternatives, but presets like "casual" are reductive since casual means different things to different users. Sparse autoencoders (Golden Gate Claude) offer a path to billion-scale presets by identifying and amplifying specific features. Ranked presets—personalized, searchable, invocable through natural language—prevent option overload. Developer-defined personalization lets developers tune features per user, impossible with fragile text prompts. Finally, he predicts a shift from evals to analytics, since many domains lack objectively correct answers, making user satisfaction metrics more relevant than correctness checks.

sections.title: Introduction and the Unbounded Products Problem
sections.summary: Ben Hylak introduces himself as founder of Dawn, which helps companies like GitHub build better AI products. He traces his obsession with unbounded products from robotics in 8th grade through SpaceX rockets to four years designing visionOS for Apple Vision Pro. AI makes products less bounded than ever—accepting text, voice, images, video, and emotional inputs—but this creates unpredictability. Users assume false capabilities, fail, and leave. Most non-technical users learn via word of mouth, not trial and error.

sections.title: Talk Overview: Past, Present, Future
sections.summary: Hylak outlines the talk's three sections: the past (how products became unbounded and what worked), the present (AI product design patterns, good and bad), and the future.

sections.title: Past: Vision Pro Design Lessons
sections.summary: Starting with how traditional software is screen-bound with predictable click/swipe/tap interactions, Hylak notes multi-touch as a key prior unbounding step. He shares three Vision Pro lessons: (1) Highlight what matters fast—home screen shows apps, people, environments. (2) Establish hierarchy—home menu, resizable windows, fullscreen. (3) Leverage familiarity—TV app mirrors tvOS, control center matches iOS; Dawn's prototype evolved from star cluster to familiar tables and graphs.

sections.title: Present: AI Design Patterns, Spreadsheets, and Presets
sections.summary: Hylak examines current AI product design. Good patterns: Dot structures chat as a journal; Perplexity structures output as a search engine; Claude artifacts pull structured output into a side panel. Bad anti-pattern: Vercel's chatbot embeds ephemeral UI sliders in chat that float away. Version control patterns (ChatGPT edit-message tree, Vercel v0) reduce fear of losing work. He adds Clay as the only real-world agent use case—spreadsheets where each column is an agent step, run like evals across rows. Examples and presets (ChatGPT suggestions, V0's explore page, Notion's tone menu) help users skip prompt engineering.

sections.title: Future: Beyond Prompt Engineering
sections.summary: Hylak argues prompt engineering will diminish, citing Linus's metaphor of driving a car with a pool noodle from the back seat. Apple's generative image UI and Figma's tone adjustment show intuitive alternatives, but presets like 'casual' are reductive—casual means different things for different companies and relationships. Sparse autoencoders (Golden Gate Claude) offer a path to billion-scale presets by identifying and amplifying specific features. Ranked presets—personalized, searchable, invocable through natural language—prevent option overload. Developer-defined personalization enables per-user tuning impossible with fragile text prompts. Finally, he predicts a shift from evals to analytics, since many domains lack objectively correct answers.
